title: Geometry — Common Core High School Math — Answer Key
id_format: S<set>-<section>-Q<number>; section is M (main), B1, B2, ... (backward), F1 or F2 (forward)
grading_rules: Match each student response to its key record by the question ID printed on the question page (for example S40-F2-Q3). The page number is the same in the Question Collection and the Answer Key. IDs are unique within one grade's collection; across collections use uid (for example G5:S40-F2-Q3).
Multiple choice and true/false: the response is correct when the chosen letter equals correct_letter, or when the student wrote the text of the correct choice.

Short answer: accept any mathematically equivalent form unless the question asks for a specific form (equivalent fractions, decimals, and mixed numbers; a ratio written as a : b, a to b, or a/b; "x = 5" or "5"; terms of an expression in any order). Units are not required unless the question asks for them.
When an answer has several parts (separated by semicolons, or with labels such as "Rate of change:"), every part must be correct.
Drawing / plotting questions (type plot): correct_answer describes what a correct drawing shows. Judge the student's drawing against it.

Drawing + written questions (type plot_text): the student draws on the figure AND writes an answer. drawing_answer describes the correct drawing and correct_answer the written answer. Both must be correct: every requested point, segment or shape in the drawing, and the written conclusion.

Answer with required work (type work): required_method says what the shown work must use. A correct final answer without that work earns partial credit only; correct work with a slip in the final answer is also partial.
Explain / describe questions: grading_note says what a correct response must include; accept any reasonable wording.
grading_note also lists other accepted answers and the work behind an answer. It is guidance for the grader, not for students.

Geometry answer forms: the grading_note of every written answer begins with "Form required:" or with "Any" (for example "Any equivalent form" or "Any valid proof"), which says what else is accepted. "Exact" means an exact value (radicals, π, fractions); a decimal approximation alone is not full credit. When rounding is allowed the note names the precision; an answer within half a unit of the last required place is correct. Units are required only when the question asks for them or the note says so.

Proofs and explanations (type work, and written answers that ask why): grade the logic, not the wording or the format. A paragraph, two-column, flow, or diagram-based argument is accepted unless the question names a format. grading_note lists the ESSENTIAL steps (every one must appear, with a valid reason), accepted alternative approaches, and common INVALID arguments (each earns no credit for that step): reasoning from how the diagram looks, measuring a drawing as proof of a general theorem, assuming what is to be proved (circular reasoning), or citing a theorem that depends on the result being proved.

Constructions (type plot): the construction must show its evidence: compass arcs and straightedge lines (or the folds, string marks, or software steps the question allows). A figure that only looks right, with no construction marks, is not full credit. Drawing tolerance: points within about 2 mm and angles within about 2° of the exact construction.

Drawings and graphs: correct_answer (or drawing_answer) states the geometric relationships a correct drawing must show (image vertices, lines, marks). Accept any drawing with those relationships; exact pencil position is not graded.
Every question has an explanation in its grading_note after the form rule; for numeric questions it shows the verified exact value and the work.

questions.set_title: Precise definitions of angle, circle, and line segment
questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: Write a precise definition of a circle. Use only the words point, plane, and distance, and words built from them.
questions.correct_answer: A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are a given distance (the radius) from a given point in that plane (the center).
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Essential: (1) ALL points, (2) in one plane, (3) at one fixed distance, (4) from one fixed point, the center. Not accepted: "a round shape" (not precise); leaving out the plane (that describes a sphere); "points within a distance" (that is a disk).

questions.set_title: Precise definitions of angle, circle, and line segment
questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: Points A and B lie on line ℓ. Which is a precise definition of segment AB?

choices.text: Points A and B together with every point C of line ℓ for which AC + CB = AB
Point A and every point of line ℓ on the same side of A as B
Every point of the plane that is closer to A than to B

questions.correct_answer: Points A and B together with every point C of line ℓ for which AC + CB = AB
questions.grading_note: A segment is its two endpoints and every point between them; "C is between A and B" means C is on the line and AC + CB = AB (distance along a line). The other choices describe line ℓ, ray AB, and a half-plane.

questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: Write a precise definition of an angle. Name its vertex and its sides in your definition.
questions.correct_answer: An angle is the figure formed by two rays that have the same endpoint. The common endpoint is the vertex, and the two rays are the sides.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent wording. Essential: two rays (not lines), one common endpoint, that endpoint named as the vertex. Not accepted: "the space between two lines", "a turn", or "two lines that cross" (two crossing lines form four angles).

questions.section_title: Test proposed definitions with counterexamples
questions.question: Proposed definition: "A circle is a set of points that are all the same distance from a point O." Give a set that fits this wording but is NOT a circle.
questions.correct_answer: For example, two points that are each 3 cm from O (or an arc of a circle, or a sphere). The definition must say ALL points at that distance, in one plane.
questions.grading_note: Any set that fits the wording but is not a whole circle: finitely many points, an arc, or a sphere.

questions.section_title: Test proposed definitions with counterexamples
questions.question: Proposed definition: "Point M is the midpoint of segment AB if AM = MB." Give a counterexample, and repair the definition.
questions.correct_answer: The top vertex of an isosceles triangle with base AB has AM = MB but is not on AB. Repair: M is the point ON segment AB with AM = MB.
questions.grading_note: Any counterexample with M off segment AB and AM = MB, plus a repair that puts M on the segment.

questions.section_title: Prove with variables that a transformation preserves or scales every distance
questions.question: Prove that T(x, y) = (x + a, y + b) preserves the distance between ANY two points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂).
questions.correct_answer: The image distance equals √((x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²), the original distance.
questions.required_method: Write both images, apply the distance formula to the images, and show that a and b cancel.
questions.grading_note: Any valid algebraic proof. Essential: images (x₁ + a, y₁ + b) and (x₂ + a, y₂ + b); the differences are x₂ - x₁ and y₂ - y₁, so the distance formula gives the same value. Invalid: checking one or two numerical examples only.

questions.correct_answer: The image distance is 3√((x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²).
questions.required_method: Write both images, apply the distance formula, and factor out 9 under the square root.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: √((3x₂ - 3x₁)² + (3y₂ - 3y₁)²) = √(9[(x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)²]) = 3·(original distance).

questions.set_title: Definitions of reflections and translations
questions.section_title: Prove from the definitions that reflections and translations keep lengths
questions.question: Points P and Q are on the same side of line ℓ, and line PQ is not perpendicular to ℓ. A reflection across ℓ maps them to P′ and Q′. Let PP′ meet ℓ at M and QQ′ meet ℓ at N. Prove that PQ = P′Q′.
questions.required_method: Use the definition (ℓ is the perpendicular bisector of PP′ and of QQ′), then two pairs of congruent triangles (SAS): PMN ≅ P′MN, then PNQ ≅ P′NQ′.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: PM = P′M and QN = Q′N with right angles at M and N (definition); triangles PMN and P′MN are congruent by SAS, so PN = P′N and ∠PNM ≅ ∠P′NM; subtracting from the right angles gives ∠PNQ ≅ ∠P′NQ′; then triangles PNQ and P′NQ′ are congruent by SAS, so PQ = P′Q′. Alternative: coordinates with ℓ as the x-axis. Invalid: "reflections preserve distance" (that is what is being proved).
questions.set_target: Define reflections and translations precisely using perpendicular bisectors, parallel lines, and segments, and use the definitions to locate images and lines of reflection

questions.grading_note: Any valid proof. Essential: PP′ ∥ QQ′ and PP′ = QQ′ in the same direction, so PP′Q′Q is a parallelogram (one pair of opposite sides parallel and congruent); opposite sides of a parallelogram are congruent, so PQ = P′Q′. Invalid: assuming translations preserve length.

questions.question: In △ABC and △DEF, AB = DE, AC = DF, and ∠A ≅ ∠D. Explain, using rigid motions, why △ABC ≅ △DEF.
questions.correct_answer: A translation, a rotation, and possibly a reflection carry A to D, B to E, and C to F, so the triangles are congruent.
questions.required_method: Translate A to D; rotate so ray AB lies on ray DE; reflect across DE if C is on the other side from F. Then explain why B lands on E and C lands on F.

questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: In △ABC and △DEF, AB = DE, BC = EF, and CA = FD. Explain, using rigid motions, why △ABC ≅ △DEF.
questions.correct_answer: A translation and a rotation carry A to D and B to E; if needed, the reflection across DE carries C′ to F.
questions.required_method: Move A to D and B to E (translation and rotation, using AB = DE). If the image C′ of C is not F, show that line DE is the perpendicular bisector of C′F, so the reflection across DE carries C′ to F.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: (1) A → D, B → E (AB = DE); (2) DC′ = DF and EC′ = EF (rigid motions keep lengths); (3) if C′ ≠ F, D and E are each equidistant from C′ and F, so line DE is the perpendicular bisector of C′F; (4) the reflection across DE fixes D and E and maps C′ to F. Alternative: C′ and F both lie on the circles centered at D and E with these radii, which meet in at most one point on each side of DE. Invalid: using angles (none are given); citing SSS to prove SSS.

questions.section_title: Prove algebraically that a dilation maps a line to a parallel line
questions.question: Prove that the dilation about the origin with scale factor k (k > 0, k ≠ 1) maps the line y = mx + b to the line y = mx + kb.
questions.correct_answer: The image of (x, mx + b) is (kx, kmx + kb), which satisfies y = mx + kb.
questions.required_method: Take any point (x, mx + b) on the line, find its image, and show the image satisfies y = mx + kb (and every point of that line is an image).
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: image (X, Y) = (kx, k(mx + b)); Y = m(kx) + kb = mX + kb; conversely (X, mX + kb) is the image of (X/k, mX/k + b). Conclusion: same slope m, so parallel when b ≠ 0, the same line when b = 0. Invalid: checking only two points of one example.

questions.set_title: Use congruence criteria to prove relationships in figures
questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: Kite ABCD has AB = AD and CB = CD. Its diagonals meet at E. Prove that AC ⊥ BD.
questions.required_method: Prove △ABC ≅ △ADC (SSS) to get ∠BAE ≅ ∠DAE; then △ABE ≅ △ADE (SAS); then the angles at E form a congruent linear pair.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: SSS (AB = AD, CB = CD, AC shared); ∠BAC ≅ ∠DAC; SAS on △ABE and △ADE (AE shared); ∠AEB ≅ ∠AED, a linear pair, so 90°. Alternative: A and C are each equidistant from B and D, so AC is the perpendicular bisector of BD.

questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: Circle C has center A and radius r, and circle D has center B and radius s. Prove that the two circles are similar.
questions.correct_answer: A translation followed by a dilation maps C onto D, so they are similar.
questions.required_method: Translate A to B, then dilate about B with scale factor s/r. Show the image of C is exactly D.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: (1) the translation maps C onto the circle with center B and radius r (distances kept); (2) the dilation about B with factor s/r maps each point at distance r from B to a point at distance s on the same ray, so onto D; (3) every point of D is reached (the inverse dilation); a similarity transformation exists. Invalid: "circles all look alike"; only checking two specific circles.

questions.domain: Geometry: Expressing Geometric Properties with Equations
questions.question: A circle has center (h, k) and radius r. Use the Pythagorean Theorem to derive the equation satisfied by every point (x, y) on the circle. The diagram shows one example, with center C(2, 1).
questions.required_method: Draw the right triangle with legs |x - h| and |y - k| and hypotenuse r.
questions.grading_note: Any valid proof (paragraph, two-column, or flow). Essential: a right triangle with horizontal leg |x - h|, vertical leg |y - k|, hypotenuse r (the distance CP); the Pythagorean Theorem gives (x - h)² + (y - k)² = r²; squaring removes the absolute values; the reasoning holds for every point on the circle (degenerate legs of length 0 included). Invalid: only checking the one example point.

questions.question: Prove that PQRS with P(-2, -1), Q(2, 1), R(1, 3), S(-3, 1) is a rectangle. Is it a square?
questions.correct_answer: Slopes PQ = RS = ½ and QR = SP = -2; adjacent products are -1, so all angles are right: a rectangle. Not a square: PQ = √20 but QR = √5.

questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: A circle of radius r is cut into many equal sectors, which are rearranged as shown. Explain why this shows that the area of the circle is πr².
questions.correct_answer: Area = (half the circumference) × r = πr · r = πr².
questions.required_method: Describe the base and height of the rearranged shape and what happens as the number of sectors grows.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: the shape approaches a parallelogram (rectangle); its height approaches r; its base is half the circumference, πr; area = πr · r = πr². Invalid: "the formula says so" or measuring one drawing.

questions.set_title: Informal arguments for the volumes of a pyramid and a cone
questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: A cube is split into three congruent pyramids that share one vertex of the cube as their apex, as shown. Use this to explain why a pyramid's volume is ⅓Bh.
questions.correct_answer: Each pyramid has the cube's base B = s² and height h = s, and the three fill the cube, so each has volume ⅓s³ = ⅓Bh.
questions.required_method: Compare each pyramid's base and height with the cube's.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: three congruent pyramids fill the cube; each has base = a face (B = s²) and height = s; so V = ⅓s³ = ⅓Bh. Extension to other pyramids by Cavalieri (cross-sections scale the same way) earns full credit but is not required.

questions.set_title: Informal arguments for the volumes of a pyramid and a cone
questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: Explain why the volume of a cone is ⅓πr²h, using pyramids.
questions.correct_answer: Pyramids with regular n-gon bases inscribed in the circle have V = ⅓Bh; as n grows, B approaches πr² and the pyramids approach the cone, so V = ⅓πr²h.
questions.required_method: Think of pyramids whose bases are regular polygons with more and more sides.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: pyramid volume ⅓Bh; base polygons approach the circle (B → πr²); the pyramids approach the cone. Alternative: Cavalieri comparison with a pyramid of equal base area and height.

questions.set_title: Use Cavalieri's principle to justify the volume of a sphere
questions.section_title: Geometry main question
questions.question: A hemisphere of radius r and a cylinder of radius r and height r with a cone removed (as shown) sit on the same plane. Use Cavalieri's principle to show that the hemisphere's volume is ⅔πr³, and conclude that a sphere has volume 4/3 πr³.
questions.correct_answer: Both cross-sections have area π(r² - y²), so the volumes are equal: πr³ - ⅓πr³ = ⅔πr³; the sphere is two hemispheres: 4/3 πr³.
questions.required_method: Compare the cross-section areas at height y.
questions.grading_note: Any valid explanation. Essential: hemisphere slice radius √(r² - y²) (Pythagorean), area π(r² - y²); the other slice is a ring with outer radius r and inner radius y (the cone radius at height y), area πr² - πy²; equal areas at every height and equal heights; Cavalieri; volume cylinder minus cone = ⅔πr³; double.
questions.set_target: Give an informal argument using Cavalieri's principle for the volume of a sphere (and other solid figures)
questions.target_skill: Give an informal argument using Cavalieri's principle for the volume of a sphere (and other solid figures)
